title: 06 — Design a Key-Value Store
html:
06 — Design a Key-Value Store

The one idea: a distributed KV store is a set of choices on the CAP trade-off. Partition with consistent hashing, replicate to N nodes, and let the client pick consistency per request with quorums (W + R > N for strong reads). Everything else — vector clocks, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, gossip — exists to survive failures in an always-writable (AP) system.

Step 1 — Scope

  • put(key, value) and get(key); values small (< 10 KB).
  • Store big data; high availability (writes succeed during failures); high scalability; automatic scaling.
  • Tunable consistency; low latency.

A single-server KV store is a hash map plus disk (compress, keep hot data in memory). The interesting problem is distributed.

Step 2 — CAP, the framing

In the presence of a network partition you must choose:

Choice Behaviour during a partition Example
CP Refuse writes/reads that can't be made consistent → some unavailability Banking balances, HBase, etcd
AP Accept writes on both sides, reconcile later → stale reads possible Dynamo, Cassandra, shopping carts
CA Not a real option — partitions happen —

PACELC adds: else (no partition), you trade latency vs consistency — which is the choice you make every day.

This design is AP with tunable consistency, Dynamo-style.

Step 3 — Deep dive: the components

3.1 Data partition

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (→ chapter 05): automatic scaling, and heterogeneous nodes get more vnodes.

3.2 Data replication

Walk the ring clockwise from the key's position and store it on the first N distinct physical servers (skip vnodes of the same server). Place replicas in different racks/zones/regions.

3.3 Quorum consensus

  • N = replicas, W = acks required for a write, R = replies required for a read.
  • The coordinator sends to all N and waits for W (or R) responses.
Config Meaning
W + R > N Read and write sets overlap → strong consistency (e.g. N=3, W=2, R=2)
R = 1, W = N Fast reads, slow/fragile writes
W = 1, R = N Fast writes, slow reads
W + R ≤ N Eventual consistency, lowest latency

3.4 Inconsistency resolution: versioning

Concurrent writes to the same key on different replicas produce conflicting versions. A vector clock — a list of [server, counter] pairs attached to each value — detects this:

  • Version X is an ancestor of Y if every counter in X ≤ the matching counter in Y → Y wins.
  • Otherwise they are siblings (concurrent) → the client (or a rule like last-write-wins) resolves.

Downsides: client-side merge complexity; clocks grow → cap their length and drop the oldest pairs.

---
title: Vector clocks — detecting conflicting writes
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant Sx as Server x
    participant Sy as Server y
    participant Sz as Server z
    C->>Sx: write D1 → [Sx,1]
    C->>Sx: write D2 → [Sx,2]
    C->>Sy: write D3 → [Sx,2],[Sy,1]
    C->>Sz: write D4 → [Sx,2],[Sz,1]
    Note over Sy,Sz: D3 and D4 conflict (siblings)
    C->>Sx: read, merge → D5 [Sx,3],[Sy,1],[Sz,1]

3.5 Failure detection: gossip

All-to-all heartbeats are O(n²). Gossip: each node keeps a membership list with heartbeat counters, periodically increments its own and sends the list to a few random peers. If a node's counter hasn't increased for a while, it's marked down — once enough peers agree.

3.6 Handling temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff

  • Sloppy quorum: instead of the strict N owners, use the first W (or R) healthy servers on the ring.
  • Hinted handoff: a stand-in server keeps the write with a hint; when the owner comes back, it hands the data over.

3.7 Handling permanent failures: anti-entropy with Merkle trees

Replicas compare Merkle trees (hash trees over key ranges). Equal roots → in sync. Otherwise descend only into differing subtrees. Data transferred is proportional to the difference, not the dataset.

3.8 Handling data-centre outage

Replicate across data centres; a DC can go dark and reads/writes continue elsewhere.

3.9 Storage engine: write and read path (LSM tree)

---
title: LSM tree — write and read paths
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph Write
        W1["Write"] --> CL["Commit log<br/>(append, fsync)"]
        CL --> MT["Memtable<br/>(sorted, in memory)"]
        MT -->|full| SS["SSTable<br/>(immutable, sorted, on disk)"]
    end
    subgraph Read
        R1["Read"] --> MT2["Memtable?"]
        MT2 -->|miss| BF["Bloom filters"]
        BF --> SS2["Only SSTables<br/>that may hold the key"]
    end
  • Writes are sequential appends → very fast.
  • Reads check the memtable, then use Bloom filters to skip SSTables that can't contain the key.
  • Background compaction merges SSTables and drops overwritten/deleted (tombstoned) values.

Step 4 — Summary table

Goal / problem Technique
Store big data Consistent hashing across servers
High availability reads Replication, multi-DC
Highly available writes Versioning + vector clocks for conflicts
Partition data Consistent hashing
Incremental scalability Consistent hashing + vnodes
Heterogeneity More vnodes for bigger servers
Tunable consistency Quorum (N, W, R)
Temporary failures Sloppy quorum, hinted handoff
Permanent failures Merkle-tree anti-entropy
DC outage Cross-DC replication

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Cosmos DB is the managed version of this design: partitioning by partition key, replication across regions, and five consistency levels (Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual) — the same dial as W/R. Session is the default and usually right: read-your-writes per client.
  • Multi-region writes in Cosmos DB use conflict resolution policies (last-writer-wins on _ts or a custom stored procedure) — the managed equivalent of sibling resolution.
  • Azure Cache for Redis is a KV store tuned the other way: in-memory, primary/replica, not quorum-based.
  • Azure Table Storage — cheap, partition-key + row-key KV at massive scale.

Review checklist

  • CAP choice stated and justified for the use case.
  • Partition (consistent hashing) + replication (N distinct nodes across zones).
  • Quorum N/W/R and what W + R > N buys.
  • Conflict detection (vector clocks) or LWW and its data-loss risk.
  • Failure handling: gossip, hinted handoff, Merkle trees.
  • LSM write path and Bloom filters on the read path.
